events.text: The morning after, you wake in a rented room above the miller's at Barley Ford and reach, out of a habit older than most kingdoms, for the river of energy that has run through you since you were young. There is no river. There is a body that is stiff from the cart, a window with a fly in it, and a field to plough. You laugh until Old Bae the miller bangs on the ceiling.

choices.text: Go and look at the field

effects.log: It is stony, sloping and badly drained. It is the first thing in a long time that you cannot fix with a thought. You love it at once.

choices.text: Lie still a while longer

effects.log: You lie there and listen to the mill wheel. For the first time in your life, nobody in the world is afraid of you.

choices.text: Go down and apologise to Old Bae

effects.log: He looks at you, grumbles, and gives you a bowl of millet porridge. "New ones always laugh," he says. "Then they work."

events.text: You were never one of the great ones, and that makes it easier and harder. You gave up a road you had only begun. At Barley Ford nobody has heard of you anyway. The miller rents you the field behind the willows, and tells you the soil is better than it looks. It is not. You are going to find that out together.

choices.text: Start clearing stones

effects.log: By evening you have a wall of them and blisters on both hands. Mortal blisters. You keep looking at them.

choices.text: Ask Old Bae how to plough

effects.log: He laughs for a full minute, then shows you. He is a good teacher. He has had a lot of practice with fools.

events.text: The road into Barley Ford feels known, though this life has never walked it. There is a field behind the willows, and you know before anyone tells you that the stones come up worst at the north end. Some life of yours laid its power down here before, and died old, and the soil remembers your hands.

choices.text: Start at the north end

effects.log: The stones come up exactly where you knew they would. Old Bae watches you work and says nothing, which is the miller's highest praise.

choices.text: Sit at the edge of the field a while

effects.log: You sit where some earlier you must have sat. The willows are older. The peace is the same.

events.text: The first harvest. The barley is thin, the rain came late, and half the north end was stones after all. You bring in every stalk by hand with a borrowed sickle, and it takes a week, and when it is done you sit on the last sheaf and eat a pear and feel as if you had broken through to a new realm. You have not. It is better.

choices.text: Take some to Old Bae

effects.log: He weighs it, sniffs, and pronounces it barley. Coming from him, it is a medal.

choices.text: Keep the best sheaf for seed

effects.log: Next year will be better. You have never been so sure of anything so small.

events.text: Years in, the field behind the willows is the best in Barley Ford, and people come to ask how. You tell them the truth: stones out, ditches dug, patience. They are disappointed. They wanted a secret. You think about all the secrets you once knew, and how none of them grew a single grain.

choices.text: Show a young farmer the ditches

effects.log: The young farmer copies them exactly. Next spring two fields in Barley Ford do not flood.

choices.text: Let them keep wanting a secret

effects.log: Someone starts a rumour that you were a great master once. You let them believe it is only a rumour.

events.text: An ordinary evening. Somebody burns the rice, somebody else blames the cat, the roof leaks in the usual corner and the household puts the usual bowl under it. You sit at the table with the lamp and the bickering and the smell of burnt rice, and think: this is what all those years of power were for. You just did not know it.

choices.text: Laugh, and eat the burnt rice

effects.log: It tastes terrible. Everyone laughs with you. It is the best meal of the year.

choices.text: Fix the roof tomorrow, at last

effects.log: You fix it. Then, missing the bowl, someone puts it back under the dry corner anyway.

events.text: The household is bigger than the house now, and noisier than the mill. In the middle of it all you are only the old one by the stove who tells stories nobody believes: once, you say, this hand could split a mountain. They roll their eyes. One of the little ones climbs into your lap and asks for the one about the mountain again.

choices.text: Tell it again

effects.log: You tell it, and make the mountain bigger every time. The little one falls asleep at the best part, as always.

choices.text: Tell a true story instead

effects.log: You tell the one about the first harvest and the pear. They like it better. So, you find, do you.

events.text: The bridge over the Barley stream washes out in the spring flood, and the village cannot reach the market. You help Old Bae and four farmers drag new timbers out of the water. Once you could have thrown the bridge across with one hand. Now it takes all six of you and a whole day, and when it is done you all stand on it, soaked and proud.

choices.text: Stamp on it to test it

effects.log: It holds. Everyone cheers as if it were a victory. It is.

choices.text: Carve the date into the rail

effects.log: You carve the date and six names. Your name is the same size as the others. You make sure of it.

events.text: A sickness comes through Barley Ford in the cold months, and you sit up nights with the families who have it, mixing the plain cures that any village grandmother knows. You remember a hundred greater cures and cannot make one of them. The plain ones work well enough, mostly. You learn to bear the times they do not.

choices.text: Sit with the worst of them

effects.log: You sit with an old farmer through the worst night. In the morning his fever breaks. He thanks you for staying, not for curing.

choices.text: Teach the young ones the plain cures

effects.log: Next winter there are six people in Barley Ford who know them. That is a kind of power too.

events.text: {npc} keeps bees on the hill above your field, and comes down in a temper one afternoon because your new ditch has flooded {his} best path. {He} is covered in mud, carrying a smoker, and very angry, and for some reason all you can think is that nobody has shouted at you in years.

choices.text: Dig {him} a new path, then and there

mem.note: dug me a path in the rain

effects.log: You dig it all afternoon. {npc} sits on the bank and supervises, and by the end is laughing at your technique.

choices.text: Offer {him} tea and an apology

effects.log: The apology is accepted. The tea is criticised. {npc} comes back the next day to criticise it again.

choices.text: Apologise, and keep to yourself

effects.log: You fix the ditch and keep your distance. Some doors, you decide, can stay shut in this life.

events.text: {npc} has been bringing you honey for two summers and criticising your tea for three. One evening, sitting on the field wall, {he} asks you straight out what you were before you came to Barley Ford. You tell the truth, all of it. {npc} listens to the end, and then says: "And now you are a farmer. Will you marry one?"

choices.text: Yes

mem.note: asked me on the field wall, and I said yes

effects.log: You marry at harvest time, under the threshing-floor lanterns. The bees are invited. Some come.

choices.text: Ask for a little more time

mem.note: took one night to say yes

effects.log: "You have time now," {npc} says. "That is the point." You realise {he} is right, and say yes the next morning.

choices.text: Say you cannot

mem.note: said no on the field wall

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, and still brings honey the next summer. Some things the quiet life does not give you.

events.text: {npc} rides into Barley Ford at noon with two hired swords, asks at the mill for the one who used to be so strong, and finds you knee-deep in the irrigation ditch. {He} has waited years for this. {He} looks at you, and looks for the power, and does not find any. "Get up," {he} says. "Fight me." You cannot. You both know it.

choices.text: Climb out of the ditch and stand there

mem.note: stood up in the mud and would not fight me

effects.log: {npc} strikes you once, hard, and you fall in the mud. You get up. {He} does not strike again. {He} rides away looking older than {he} came.

choices.text: Offer {him} a bowl of water

mem.note: gave me water instead of a fight

effects.log: {npc} stares at the bowl for a long time. Then {he} drinks it, and sits on your field wall, and the two of you talk about the old days until dark.

choices.text: Reach for the power out of habit

mem.note: reached for a power that was gone

effects.log: Nothing comes. {npc} sees you reach and find nothing, and laughs, and leaves you there. The laugh stays with you for a while.

events.text: {npc} comes to Barley Ford alone, at night, and stands at the edge of your field in the moonlight for an hour before speaking. "They told me you gave it all up," {he} says at last. "I did not believe them. I came to see for myself." {He} could kill you with one hand. Everyone in the house is asleep.

choices.text: Tell {him} it is true, and why

mem.note: told me the truth in the moonlight

effects.log: You talk all night. At dawn {npc} walks away without having touched you, and you never learn what {he} decided.

choices.text: Ask {him} not to wake the house

mem.note: asked me only to let the house sleep

effects.log: {npc} looks at the dark windows and something in {his} face gives way. "I will not," {he} says, and goes.

choices.text: Reach for the power

mem.note: tried to reach a power that was gone

effects.log: There is nothing to reach. {npc} watches you try, and pities you, which is worse than anything {he} came to do.

events.text: {npc} brings witnesses this time: a crowd of young fighters from the city who have heard the stories and want to see the great one humbled. {He} knocks the hoe out of your hands in front of the whole village and waits for you to beg. Old Bae comes out of the mill with a flour sack in each fist, and stands beside you. So do the four farmers who built the bridge.

choices.text: Thank them, and send them home

mem.note: had a whole village at the back

effects.log: They will not go. {npc} looks at a mortal village standing between {him} and you, and finds {he} has no stomach for it.

choices.text: Pick up the hoe and go back to work

mem.note: turned their back on me and hoed a row

effects.log: You turn your back on {him} and hoe the next row. The crowd of young fighters falls silent. Some of them will remember this longer than any duel.

events.text: A young fighter named Do Hyeon arrives at Barley Ford with a sword too good for a beginner and a list of old masters to beat. Your name is at the top. Do Hyeon finds you mending a fence, looks at you for a long time, and says: "I came to beat you. There is nothing here to beat."

choices.text: Agree, and hand over the hammer

effects.log: Do Hyeon mends the fence with you all afternoon, confused, and leaves at dusk, crossing your name off the list with care.

choices.text: Tell Do Hyeon what the list is worth

effects.log: "Nothing, at the end," you say. "Ask me how I know." Do Hyeon asks. It takes all night. The list goes into your stove.

choices.text: Feel for the old strength

effects.log: It is not there. Do Hyeon sees your hand close on nothing and looks away, embarrassed for you. You are embarrassed too.

events.text: Gwak Cheol, the Black Hook, an old killer you beat a long time ago, finds you at the market with a basket of eggs. He has a hook where his right hand used to be and twenty years of waiting in his face. He walks you behind the tannery, very politely, and asks you to fight. You put the eggs down first, carefully, so they will not break.

choices.text: Stand still and let him do what he came for

effects.log: He hits you once, then stares at the eggs, then at you. "You really did give it up," he says, and something in him gives up too.

choices.text: Ask him if he is hungry

effects.log: He is. You cook him eggs behind the tannery. The Black Hook eats them with his good hand, and does not say thank you, and does not hurt you.

choices.text: Reach for the power

effects.log: Nothing answers. Gwak Cheol laughs, takes your eggs, and leaves you sitting in the alley. It is a small loss, and it stays with you.

events.text: You know it the way farmers know weather. One autumn evening you ask to be carried out to the field wall, and the whole household comes, and sits with you in the long light over the barley. Someone has brought the burnt-rice pot for luck. Nobody says what everyone knows. You have never been so rich in your life.

choices.text: Tell them the story of the mountain one more time

effects.log: You make the mountain enormous. They laugh. Somebody cries. The barley moves in the wind like a held breath.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: you would choose this again

effects.log: "Every time," you say, and mean every life. The light goes down over Barley Ford slowly, the way it always has.

events.text: You know it the way farmers know weather. One autumn evening you sit on the field wall by yourself, with Old Bae's grandson bringing you a cup of tea and staying to drink one too. The barley is good this year. You gave up the whole sky for a field, and you look at it now and do not regret one stalk.

choices.text: Give the boy the field

effects.log: "It is yours after," you tell him. He does not understand yet. He will, one harvest.

choices.text: Sit until the stars come out

effects.log: You sit until the stars come out. You used to walk among them. They look better from here.

events.text: Passing a village you have never seen, you stop at the edge of a barley field and cannot move on. Your hands know the weight of a sickle they have never held. Somewhere a past life of yours laid every power down and died old in a field like this one, and was happy. You did not know a soul could remember happiness. It can.

choices.text: Ask the farmer if you may help a while

effects.log: You bring in a row of barley for a stranger, badly, joyfully. The farmer gives you a pear, which feels like the right ending.

choices.text: Walk on, lighter

effects.log: You walk on. All the power in the world is still out there for you to chase. You find you are in less of a hurry.

events.text: In a dream you open your hand and let everything in it go, and you are not afraid. You wake with mud under your fingernails and the smell of a mill in the room. A past life of yours chose to lay its power down. This one does not have to. It is good to know that it could.

choices.text: Lie still and remember the mill

effects.log: You can hear the wheel turning, very far away, in another life. It keeps time for you all day.

choices.text: Get up and train harder

effects.log: If you ever lay it down, you think, it should be something worth laying down.
